articles.title: Marriage as Slavery: Oroonoko, the Slave Trade, and the Origins of English Feminism
articles.abstract: This article investigates Mary Astell’s controversial comparison of marriage to slavery. While existing scholarship situates this analogy within the neo-Roman republican framework, which defined slavery as subjection to absolute rule, I investigate another paradigm: the transatlantic slave trade. To make this case, the article traces the influence of Aphra Behn’s Oroonoko (1688) on early feminist thought. By foregrounding the market logic underpinning chattel slavery, Behn popularized the idea that slavery’s harms were rooted, not in absolute power, but in the commodification of human beings. Astell appropriated this insight, showing that marriage resembled slavery not because husbands wielded power over wives but because the institution had been commodified: women were treated as things to be bought and sold. In uncovering this genealogy of feminist thought, the article highlights the enduring contributions of the “first” English feminists—insights that are entangled with, and shaped by, the development of the slave trade.

articles.title: The Representation Trap: How Minority Power Shapes Electoral Politics in India
articles.abstract: Liberal democracy requires that minority groups be represented in politics. This article argues that minority representation can also generate headwinds for political inclusion by dividing the minority group and consolidating the dominant group. I study the combination of these processes, termed the representation trap, through a mixed-methods examination of Muslims in India. Analyses of election results and an original survey of Hindu and Muslim voters show that electing a Muslim representative divides Muslim votes across an increased share of coethnic candidates and consolidates Hindu votes for the majoritarian party in the subsequent election. Qualitative evidence and a vignette experiment trace these patterns to two mechanisms: sub-identity activation among Muslims and super-ordinate identity mobilization among Hindus. By showing how representation restructures elite and voter behavior within both minority and dominant groups, the article highlights the dynamic nature of ethnic politics and complicates the view of minorities as politically unified.

articles.title: What Would It Mean to Democratize Finance? An Evaluation of Divergent Conceptions of Democracy and Finance
articles.abstract: Calls to “democratize finance” abound today. Yet this apparent consensus obscures sharply divergent conceptions of both democracy and finance. This article maps these demands along two axes, distinguishing between access- and power-based conceptions of democracy, and between three dimensions of finance: payment, capital markets, and banking. We then develop three normative claims. First, we argue that conceptions that reduce democratization to expanded market access are not merely insufficient but, when applied to speculative capital markets, amount to predatory inclusion. Second, thicker accounts of democratization as equal inclusion are normatively more promising but internally unstable, as their democratic commitments generate pressures toward power sharing. Third, the most plausible conceptions of democratizing finance are power-centered and involve greater public control over credit creation and allocation. Rather than defending a single institutional solution, the article assesses a range of reform proposals while specifying a normative threshold for evaluating what it would mean to democratize finance.

articles.title: Democratic Accountability with Citizen Coproduction
articles.authors: JIE MA, KEITH E. SCHNAKENBERG, IAN R. TURNER
articles.abstract: Many policies require citizens to actively participate in their implementation in order to be successful, a situation referred to as citizen coproduction. Though citizen coproduction is necessary in many policy areas, it could create difficulties for democratic accountability because citizens and politicians share responsibility for policy failures and attribution of blame may be difficult. We analyze the problem of democratic accountability with citizen coproduction in the context of a model in which politicians, who vary with respect to their competence at selecting policies, choose whether to implement policies whose success depends on citizen coproduction choices. For citizens, the problem is one of attribution: when coproduction is low, it may be hard to select good incumbents because policy failures are frequent even when policy choices are good. Incumbents anticipate these effects, which sometimes implies that they are less likely to choose reforms when they are more likely to be successful.

articles.title: Critical Ties: How NGOs Become Reliable Information Suppliers to International Organizations
articles.authors: Florencia Montal, Gino Pauselli, María-José Urzúa
articles.abstract: International organizations (IOs) monitor compliance with international norms but public criticism of member states remains discretionary. We argue that such criticism depends not only on mandates or political incentives, but on whether IOs can access information they deem credible. This credibility is socially produced. Through repeated interaction, IO staff develop trust in specific local non-governmental organizations (NGOs), which become reliable conduits of mandate-aligned and verifiable information. These trust-based ties reduce uncertainty and reputational risk, enabling public criticism. We test this argument using original data on press releases and NGO participation in public hearings at the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights from 1996 to 2020. Combining statistical analysis, an instrumental variable strategy, text analysis, and interview evidence, we show that the Commission is more likely to issue and to sharpen critical press releases when it has established ties with local NGOs focused on the relevant country and issue.

articles.title: The Threshold Effect: Preference Falsification Versus Weak Preferences in Russian War Support
articles.authors: Isabelle DeSisto, Grigore Pop-Eleches, Jacob R. Tucker
articles.abstract: How reliable are surveys in autocracies? Using data from wartime Russia, we show why list experiments – commonly used to detect preference falsification – do not always reveal hidden dissent. We identify and test what we call the ‘threshold effect’: respondents may report support for a sensitive item in a direct question but omit it in a list experiment, not because they are lying, but because the list format can create a higher threshold for expressing support. We provide direct evidence of this effect and use two approaches to distinguish preference falsification from weak preferences. Both suggest that outright lying in Russia is limited, but many attitudes are weak and easily shaped by question framing. We conclude that while many Russians genuinely support the war against Ukraine, this support is shallow. Our findings suggest that researchers should take care when designing and interpreting survey questions that measure sensitive attitudes using indirect methods.

articles.title: The Legacy of Mexico’s Drug War on Youth Political Attitudes
articles.abstract: How does childhood exposure to large-scale criminal violence and militarized law enforcement shape political attitudes and behavior? We examine the case of Mexico’s drug war, where a generation has been raised amidst the country’s most violent conflict in over a century. Surveying nearly 3,000 urban youth to measure their political and interpersonal trust, we matched respondents to historical data on criminal violence and military confrontations and operations in their childhood municipalities. Disentangling the effects of criminal violence and military interventions, we find that exposure to homicidal violence during childhood erodes interpersonal trust and trust in law enforcement, while military interventions – especially those involving violent confrontations – broadly undermine trust in federal security institutions and generate political backlash against the parties that governed Mexico during the exposure period. These findings have important implications for young democracies affected by high crime and violence and advance our understanding of how criminal wars influence political socialization.

articles.title: When, Where, and Why Might Elected Political Elites Reach for Democratic Innovations?
articles.authors: Şule Yaylacı, Mark Warren, Edana Beauvais
articles.abstract: Electoral democracies are under strain. Elections and conventional relations of representation between elected politicians and citizens do not seem to be providing sufficient legitimacy for democratic governance. In principle, democratic innovations such as deliberative minipublics or participatory budgeting could supplement electoral systems so that they function more democratically. But elected representatives may resist these innovations due to unfamiliarity, perceived threats to their power, and the belief that traditional electoral methods suffice for democratic legitimacy. This paper theorizes the potential incentives for elected officials to adopt democratic innovations, examining the conditions under which innovations might align with their interests. Democratic deficits may, and often do, present electoral risks and challenges. By mapping democratic deficits onto elite incentives, we suggest when, where, and why the strategic motivations of elected officials might align with democratic innovations. We illustrate the theory with examples of democratic innovations drawn primarily from the Participedia database. We conclude that strategies for deepening democracy should include understanding how democratic innovations relate to incentives structured by electoral institutions, so that innovations might supplement rather than compete with electoral democracy.

articles.title: How left-wing parties shape the voting gender gap across Western Europe
articles.abstract: Empirical evidence suggests that the traditional gender gap in voting behaviour has been reversed in many advanced democracies. Cultural and structural factors have led the younger generations of women to shift from voting more conservatively than men to being more likely to support left-wing parties. Although these transformations have affected virtually all advanced democracies, empirical evidence shows that this gap is not uniform across time and space; there is significant variation in both the presence and strength of the association. In this paper, we argue that this variability can be partly explained by the role of left-wing political parties. In particular, we hypothesise that the modern gender gap is stronger when left-wing parties adopt progressive positions on both the socio-cultural and economic dimensions of politics. To test these hypotheses, 19 Western European countries are analysed using a dataset that integrates individual-level data from the European Social Survey (Waves 1–10) with party-level data from the Comparative Manifesto Project, covering 85 elections between 1999 and 2021. The results reveal that the modern gender gap is shaped by party positioning, with left-wing parties’ positions on both the economic and, most relevantly, the socio-cultural dimension playing a key role in reinforcing or mitigating gendered voting patterns.

articles.title: The making of strange bedfellows: spatial diffusion in unorthodox coalition building
articles.authors: Gissur Ó Erlingsson, Emanuel Wittberg, Hanna Emilia Bäck, Assar Wixe
articles.abstract: Why do ideologically distant political adversaries sometimes choose to govern together? This article advances research on coalition formation in parliamentary democracies by introducing a diffusion-of-innovation perspective. We argue that cooperation between political archenemies can spread spatially as parties learn from nearby cases. When sister parties in adjacent jurisdictions successfully form such coalitions without electoral punishment or sanction from national leaderships, the normative barriers to similar cooperation are weakened. In this way, unorthodox coalitions become politically imaginable and strategically viable through processes of observation, emulation, and learning. We test this argument in the context of Swedish local government, where an extraordinary transformation has occurred over the past few decades. Historically, cooperation between the Social Democrats and the Moderates – the two dominant rivals for national power – has been virtually unthinkable. Today, however, these former adversaries co-govern in nearly one-fifth of Sweden’s 290 municipalities. This shift in coalition behaviour challenges core expectations in coalition theory, which predict alliances between ideologically proximate parties. Drawing on a unique panel dataset covering eight local election cycles (1994–2022), we employ complementary log-log regression models to test whether exposure to unorthodox coalitions in the surrounding regional environment increases the likelihood of similar coalition formation. The analysis reveals clear evidence of hierarchical regional contagion: Social Democrat–Moderate coalitions are significantly more likely to emerge in administrative regions where similar arrangements existed in the previous term. These findings suggest that coalition formation is a socially embedded process of spatial learning, offering a new account of how political cooperation evolves across space.

articles.title: Online privacy protection: How the varieties of democracy matter
articles.abstract: Digital technologies have enabled the gathering, storing, and processing of large amounts of data in increasing and unprecedented ways. This has triggered concerns regarding governments’ ability to harvest vast amounts of information on citizens and the consequences of this surveillance on democracy. The reliance of many democracies on digital (surveillance) technologies in response to the 2019 Coronavirus pandemic has amplified these concerns. While most studies focus on how privacy violations affect democracy, this study analyzes how variations in democracy affect the legal protection of citizens’ rights. We rely on data from the varieties of democracy to capture this variation and on data from the Digital Society Project to measure variations in online privacy protection laws. Our results point to a complex and partially unexpected relationship between democracy, its different dimensions, and online privacy protection laws in democratic regimes. The quality of democracy is positively associated with protective online privacy laws in typical times, but changes in democratic quality in the years preceding the pandemic did not affect changes in online privacy laws during the pandemic. However, the relationship between the different dimensions of democracy and privacy laws is more complex, and our results show that egalitarianism and participation are more important than liberalism in protecting online privacy laws. We conclude with a discussion of the relevance of these results to policy.

articles.title: Pocketbook politics and climate action: How economic strain reduces support for green parties
articles.abstract: Why do green parties struggle electorally despite overwhelming public support for climate action? While macro-level studies suggest that green party performance is shaped by economic conditions, the micro-level mechanisms driving this relationship remain unclear. This paper investigates whether personal economic strain reduces support for green parties and reshapes climate-related political attitudes. Leveraging rich panel data from Germany (2016–2024), I combine long-term correlational analysis with a difference-in-differences design exploiting the war-related 2022 surge in consumer prices. Voters facing financial hardship consistently evaluate the Greens more negatively and shift their political attention toward inflation and economic growth, while deprioritizing climate protection. However, evidence on vote intentions is mixed. These findings contribute to debates on green party support and the distributive politics of climate action, highlighting the relevance of voters’ pocketbooks and the need for green parties to convincingly address material concerns to ensure electoral success.

articles.title: The party soldier, the young careerist, and the outsider: How distinctive career paths affect party dissent
articles.abstract: Parties are not unified entities, yet research on intra-party dissent has focused on legislators while overlooking the broader pool of candidates and the distinct career paths that bring them into politics. Drawing on theories of careerism, representation, and spatial competition, I argue that pre-parliamentary careers shape both whether candidates dissent from their party and in which direction. Using the Comparative Candidates Survey across thirteen country-elections, I find that party soldiers with local roots are the most loyal, whereas young careerists who have never worked outside politics are the most likely to dissent. Crucially, when careerists break with their party, they move toward the centre rather than the extremes, and they do so most when their electoral chances are high. These findings link the professionalisation of political careers to party cohesion and candidate-voter congruence.

articles.title: Partisan differentiation in legislative texts in South Korea: Agenda selection, framing, and partisan classifiability in the 21st national assembly
articles.abstract: How do parties translate their ideological identities into the language of legislation? This study analyzes 22,964 member-sponsored bills from the Democratic Party of Korea and the People Power Party in the 21st Korean National Assembly, decomposing partisan differences into three dimensions: agenda setting, framing, and partisan classifiability. The study finds significant divergence in topic distributions across parties, with the Democratic Party prioritizing judicial reform and labor rights while the People Power Party emphasizes real estate taxation and regional development. More substantively novel is the evidence for within-topic framing differences: even after agenda composition is held constant, keyword contrasts within shared policy domains reveal recurring asymmetries in problem diagnosis and justificatory language. A text-only classification model further confirms that partisan identity is consistently encoded in legislative texts. These findings indicate that agenda selection and within-topic framing combine to produce a consistent partisan signal. Party discipline, decentralized incentives for position-taking, and ideological polarization constitute plausible institutional and political conditions under which such a pattern may emerge, with broader implications for comparative research on party-centered democracies.

articles.title: Digitalisation without democratisation: Organisational conditions for deliberative override capacity in European parties
articles.abstract: Contemporary political parties are digitalising their internal processes at an accelerating rate, yet higher levels of digitalisation do not consistently translate into deeper internal democracy. This article builds a diagnostic framework around deliberative override capacity (DOC), the organisational conditions under which members can access, contest, and reverse technically mediated decisions. Combining an exploratory analysis of the DIGIPART dataset (n = 76) with a theory-building statutory analysis of 18 parties across seven countries, we find that only two parties exhibit the full statutory configuration associated with robust DOC, while most combine formal participatory commitments with executive or proprietary control of the digital infrastructure. A DOC proxy applied to the seventy-six parties indicates that DOC captures variation existing indices do not: parties scoring highly on democratic digital-innovation indices may nonetheless exhibit governance indeterminacy, that is, a formal participatory commitment without any statutory specification of who controls the digital infrastructure. We develop a heuristic typology of override configurations across ideological families and draw out its implications for party-organisation research and party law. The design is configurational and cross-sectional; we identify co-occurrence patterns rather than causal effects.

articles.title: Full boat, empty boat: The politics of maritime migration and its racial spectres
A complex arc of engagement: Shifting psychological trajectories of international solidarity during sustained geopolitical conflict
articles.authors: Vivian P. Ta‐Johnson, A. Burcu Bayram
articles.abstract: How do international audiences psychologically engage with prolonged geopolitical conflicts on social media? Drawing on 1.2+ million English‐language tweets posted during the first 10 months of the Russia–Ukraine war, this study examines temporal shifts in engagement, emotion, existential concern, cognition, and psychological distance reflected through language. Results identified a clear psychological arc across the conflict. Discourse in the earliest phase was characterized by strong active engagement, heightened negative emotion, increased focus on death, conflict, and morality, and greater cognitive effort aimed at making sense of unfolding events. As the war persisted, these indicators declined and were replaced by shorter posts, fewer retweets, reduced existential focus, and simpler emotional and cognitive expression, consistent with attention fatigue and chronic crisis adaptation. Unexpectedly, psychological distance decreased over time, suggesting that users expressed themselves in more personal, spontaneous ways as the conflict became an enduring part of the digital environment. This challenges the view that declining engagement signals general disengagement and instead reveals a shift toward more grounded, personally meaningful forms of involvement. Findings illuminate the dynamic psychological processes through which publics respond to sustained conflict and highlight implications for political communication, humanitarian outreach, and crisis messaging strategies across the lifespan of international crises.

articles.title: From identity to caring: A 44‐country examination of the role of global social identifications in concern for global issues
articles.authors: Marta Penczek, Katarzyna Hamer, Katarzyna Branowska, Zuzanna Zdanowicz, Laura Loy, David Sparkman, Maria Baran, Paul Bertin, Margarida Carmona, Theofilos Gkinopoulos, Justin Hackett, Rita Guerra, Anna Wlodarczyk, Karolina Marcinkowska, Bartek Nowak, Grace Akello, Flavia Albarello, Mujeeba Ashraf, Maja Bednarowicz, Nora C. Nagy, Kenzo Nera, Boglarka Nyul, Ayu Okvitawanli, James Osinde, Emrah Özsoy, Jorge Palacio, Ondrey Pešout, Anna‐Maija Pirttilä‐Backman, Vivien Pong, Erico Rentería, Dayana Restrepo, Adil Samekin, Heyla Selim, Denis Sindic, Alexa Spence, Sabrina Stöckli, Tam Kim‐Pong, Joaquín Ungaretti, Illia Yahiiaiev, Yelena Yemelyanova
articles.abstract: Previous research suggests that people who identify with global communities tend to show greater concern for global challenges. Using student samples from 44 countries across different cultural clusters ( N = 13,055), we examined whether (1) three forms of dispositional global social identification (GSI, with all humanity, citizens of the world, and people all over the world) are related to concern for global issues, (2) situational activation of these identifications increases such concern, (3) country‐level traditional and survival values are negatively associated with global concern, and (4) these values moderate the GSI–concern link. Both dispositional and situational GSIs positively predicted global concern. Situational activation showed inconsistent effects, whereas dispositional GSIs demonstrated moderate and consistent associations with global concern across the full sample and most countries. Overall, dispositional forms of GSI appeared more influential than situational ones. Contrary to expectations, traditional values (and survival values—marginally) were positively related to global concern and showed no evidence of moderating GSI–concern associations. Additional analyses showed the indices of GDP per capita, Human Development, Gini, and poverty as robust predictors of global concern. We discuss how these findings refine claims about the universality of global identification outcomes and highlight the importance of socio‐cultural context in shaping such concern.

articles.title: Bad news for (young) gamers: Using gaming platforms as news sources is more intimately associated with radical belief dispositions than other online spaces
articles.authors: Simon Greipl, Ulrike Schwertberger, Diana Rieger, Brigitte Naderer
articles.abstract: This study explores how digital news use among young Europeans links to radical belief dispositions, particularly within gaming platforms and messengers, where socio‐affective dynamics shape engagement with political information. We argue that online groups are an overlooked locus for biased information processing and the normalization of extremist worldviews. The conflation of an increasingly fragmented online news space with the inherently politicized gaming cosmos can relate to amplified problematic worldviews based on shared activity, identity, and reality. Based on a cross‐country survey ( N = 1489; eight European countries), we compare (the use of) gaming, messenger apps, social media, and traditional media for news in terms of how they afford problematic forms of collectivity, particularly in relation to social, cynical, and radical epistemologies. We find a robust correlation between news use and a set of radical belief dispositions, prominently with messenger apps, but even more so in gaming‐related online environments—less so on social media and none with traditional news use. Notably, a mediation analysis suggests that shared meaning‐making exhibits a negative rather than a positive indirect association with radical belief dispositions. We discuss the complex interplay of how individual factors and platform architectures connect with news engagement utilizing a vulnerability‐affordance framework.

articles.title: Contact as collective action: Positive and negative contact experiences of disadvantaged group members
articles.authors: Fiona Kazarovytska, Micha Hilbert, Dana Ionescu
articles.abstract: Intergroup contact programs worldwide strive to combat prejudice by promoting encounters between socially advantaged and disadvantaged groups. Despite their prevalence, little is known about how disadvantaged group members experience participation in such programs. We present qualitative field data from the German contact program Meet a Jew . In this program, Jewish volunteers engage in dialogue with attendees and share insights into their Jewish life to address antisemitism. Drawing on N = 450 volunteer responses (age range: 16–77 years) collected over five years (2020–2025), we examine the positive and negative experiences of volunteers with the arranged encounters. A qualitative content analysis shows that volunteers experienced contact as positive when their engagement and perspectives were met with interest, their efforts were socially recognized, and they perceived their engagement as effective in contributing to social change. However, volunteers also reported negative experiences, including disinterest from attendees, interference by authorities, and various conflicts. By providing the perspective of Jewish individuals who are both targets of prejudice and actors of prejudice reduction, we address the understudied perspective of disadvantaged group members who engage in contact interventions as agents of collective action. We discuss how our work contributes to contact theory and advances research on social change.

articles.title: The effects of participating in government-led citizens’ assemblies
articles.authors: Mariana C. Duarte, Jorge M. Fernandes, Miguel M. Pereira
articles.abstract: Contemporary democracies face growing public disaffection and mistrust. Governments have tried to revert these trends by promoting participatory governance. Prior studies established how deliberation can empower citizens. However, whether these effects hold in real-life initiatives initiated by partisan governments remains unclear. We test the ability of citizens’ assemblies to foster democratic attitudes in a natural experiment leveraging the random selection of participants to Lisbon’s citizens’ assemblies Participation led to an increase in issue knowledge and salience, external political efficacy and institutional trust. However, it did not impact internal political efficacy nor helped citizens better recognize the challenges of collective decision-making. The results hold for two assembly editions and reveal the potential of government-led participatory initiatives to reconnect citizens with democracy.

articles.title: Electoral timing and local user charges: evidence from sewerage tariffs in Japan
Why chief executives (dis)obey the law
articles.authors: Daniel A. Farber, Jonathan S. Gould
articles.abstract: When and why will chief executives obey the law, and when and why will they violate it? This article constructs a general framework for analyzing legal (non)compliance by a rational chief executive. It evaluates benefits and costs that might result from executive lawbreaking by reference to three types of objectives that chief executives may have: policy and governance objectives, electoral and political objectives, and personal objectives. Assessing the benefits and costs of lawbreaking requires examining not only the chief executive but also how other actors respond to lawbreaking, including legislatures, courts, civil servants, and market actors. Additional factors, such as the chief executive’s discount rate and risk tolerance, also bear on benefits and costs. Understanding the determinants of executive obedience or disobedience generates both hypotheses for further research and a potential reform agenda for those worried about executive lawbreaking.

articles.title: Coloring in the lines: the role of segregation and majority-minority districts in local descriptive representation
articles.abstract: The urban politics literature finds municipal elections are highly racialized, but it is unclear how this is reflected in redistricting. I analyze the implementation of majority-minority districts in 133 US cities during the 2010 redistricting cycle. I find that in cities where Black or Hispanic citizens are minorities, they are proportionally underrepresented in city council districts, but are overrepresented in cities where they make up the majority. To isolate the role of residential segregation, I use a Monte Carlo algorithm to sample from the underlying distribution of plausible maps. The proportion of Hispanic-majority districts implemented generally matches median simulated plans, but nearly one-third of cities implemented more Black-majority districts than the median simulation. The proportion of Black city council members positively predicts the gap between the median proportion of majority-minority districts simulated and the proportion implemented. I then link this data to the electoral outcomes of racially identified candidates. I find that majority-minority and majority-White districts elect co-racial or co-ethnic candidates in over 75% of elections (n = 2,434). Finally, I predict the number of Black and Hispanic councilors elected under simulated plans. Implemented plans led to an estimated 9.5% more Black councilors on average, but roughly the same number of Hispanic councilors.
